doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: Trading fours, soloing and listening on the bandstand
summary: Harper composes solos like Max Roach, bases trading on the previous player, and goes in open to the other musicians.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you ever, when you’re doing those four bar breaks, eight bar breaks or whatever, do you plan ahead for the next break? There was a guy, I read a quote, someone in the Washington Post reviewing, you were playing with someone and it said “wonderfully orchestrated solos.”

No I’m kind of like — because Max was such a big influence on me too. That was my entrance into jazz. So, and him and all those guys, but I mean him and Higgins both had a big influence on me as well as Elvin and a bunch of other guys, Frankie Dunlop, Billy Hart. So when it comes to solos I’m still trying to compose, you know, like Max. I’m trying to say something. So in my solos, if I’ve got a solo I may have some ideas and then I’ll go forthwith, and then from that something else comes. But on the trading, trading is, for me it’s always based on what the horn player plays or the piano player plays, whoever is taking the fours before me. Because if they’ve said something I’m either trying to continue the statement or answer the statement. So sometimes rhythmically I may hear something in what they played and I may borrow from or take that and start it and go from there. Sometimes it can be a conversation. And then everybody looks and says wow, he hears me. You know what I mean? And then all the doors start opening up with everybody, everybody’s giving and taking. It’s a wonderful thing playing music. If you think about it, all those things are fundamentals for life. Because you know what it does to somebody when they realize and they find out somebody hears me. I’ve talked and he’s listening. For families, for everything else. Some of it doesn’t happen as much as it needs to, even in society. You know that’s a lot of what’s going on. People are talking and they feel like nobody’s listening. Okay like who hears me? And that’s what happens on the bandstand a lot of times. I always tell a lot of my students, once you start playing with people, people you’ve never played with before, you’re going to find that once they know that you’re listening and you hear them it’s going to open up a door. I mean it always happens. You know you might be playing with somebody and they’re just thinking about playing the music. And all of a sudden they play something and you catch it and all of a sudden they look up, oh, we’re conversating. You know?

I like that word. Conversating. And I have found that the more in tune the rhythm section is the easier it is to play, or the less hard. You’re not feeling like you’re trying to drag people with you or something. It becomes a group effort. So tonight, when you play with — three of the four other guys in the band are in their 70s and 80s. Do you go into that situation thinking I need to change my playing? Or, as opposed to when you might be working with your own quintet?

I try to mostly go into situations, like I told you, I try to, before I walk out that door I try to make sure look empty my glass so I can come with an empty cup and bring something back. If you’re going to a buffet and you’ve got two sandwiches in your bag, you know what I mean? So I try to make sure I’m open so I can receive. I can see. It’s like a doctor coming in and before he’s even seen you he’s already got a diagnosis. You don’t want to be that doctor. You want to be a doctor, you know, somebody just told him, it’s this. You want to go look and see for yourself. Because it may not be. It may just be some

symptoms. You know. So you want to go get a good idea for yourself. If you already go with things in mind you’ve already narrowed your scope. So I try to just, like I say, be open, empty myself, so I can go and see what it is or what I’m working with and where it’s going to go. Because then maybe we can take things to some different places.
